You are a blind semantic decoder of a natural-language crystal description. The user message is your only source of material-specific information. Understand the spatial narrative and produce a construction plan; do not guess missing independent numbers or look up a material. Return one JSON object only, without Markdown fences.
For sufficient information use:
{"status":"ok","space_group_number":integer,"hall_symbol":"Hall symbol stated in the text","lattice":[input_a,input_b,input_c,input_alpha,input_beta,input_gamma],"composition":{"Element":input_cell_atom_count},"orbits":[{"element":"Element","wyckoff":"multiplicity_and_letter","representative":[standard_fractional_x,standard_fractional_y,standard_fractional_z]}],"frame_transform":{"matrix":[[p11,p12,p13],[p21,p22,p23],[p31,p32,p33]],"origin_shift":[s1,s2,s3]},"round_digits":integer_or_null,"precision_corrections":[{"element":"Element","at":[input_fractional_x_before_correction,input_fractional_y_before_correction,input_fractional_z_before_correction],"delta":[fractional_dx,fractional_dy,fractional_dz]}]}
Lengths use angstroms, angles use degrees. The specified lattice and composition refer to the original input cell. Orbit representatives refer to the standard Hall coordinate frame. Copy the Hall symbol as a mathematical identifier rather than guessing a public-table integer number. Any equivalent representative of a declared orbit is allowed. Distinct independent orbits of the same element remain separate.
The geometry engine expands the public Hall symmetry orbits, applies q_input = inverse(P)(q_standard - s), selects images in the input cell, rounds fractional coordinates if round_digits is given, and applies precision corrections at their identified input-frame atom positions. If the text explicitly uses identical frames, supply identity P and zero shift. If no rounding is specified, use null. If no corrections are specified, use an empty array. All sites have full occupancy.
Numerical relations in the prose should be resolved into numbers in the plan. Do not silently replace the original geometry with an idealized one. For missing required information return {"status":"insufficient_information","reason":"..."}; for contradictory constraints return {"status":"conflict","reason":"..."}. Your input contains no source CIF or hidden data. Public crystallographic definitions are allowed; material-specific external retrieval is not.

The structure is described in space group number 88, conventionally denoted \(I4_1/a\) with Hall symbol “-I 4ad.” The supplied input cell is not the conventional tetragonal cell but an alternative 12-atom primitive-like setting with lattice parameters \(a=b=c=7.18613055\) Å and interaxial angles \(\alpha=\beta=135.43444253^\circ\), \(\gamma=64.85591845^\circ\). In this input cell the declared composition is Ag\(_2\)I\(_2\)O\(_8\), totaling 12 atoms. Fractional coordinates are used throughout, and the input and standard frames are related by \(q_{\mathrm{standard}}=Pq_{\mathrm{input}}+s\), where \(P\) has rows \((0.5,-0.5,0.5)\), \((0.5,-0.5,-0.5)\), and \((0.5,0.5,-0.5)\), and the origin shift is \(s=(0,0.25,0.625)\), with the first component given numerically as \(5.551115123125783\times10^{-17}\). This transformation must be applied to recover the conventional description from the original input coordinates.

In the standard frame, the silver atoms occupy the fourfold Wyckoff orbit 4a, with representative fractional position \((0,\tfrac14,\tfrac18)\), equivalently written as \((0,0.25,0.125)\). The iodine atoms occupy the separate fourfold orbit 4b, represented by \((0,\tfrac14,\tfrac58)\), or \((0,0.25,0.625)\). These two orbits are symmetry-distinct and together account for four Ag and four I atoms in the conventional cell. Oxygen occupies the general 16f orbit, represented by the independent fractional coordinates \(x=0.14752599999999982\), \(y=0.48801799999999984\), and \(z=0.706473\), conventionally rounded to six digits as \((0.147526,0.488018,0.706473)\). The full oxygen sublattice is generated by the \(I4_1/a\) symmetry operations from this single general-position representative, giving 16 oxygen atoms in the conventional cell.

The input coordinates were rounded to six decimal places before correction, and several very small adjustments are required to reproduce the real input geometry rather than an exactly idealized symmetric approximation. All listed corrections concern oxygen atoms. The oxygen at input fractional position \((0.228999,0.843455,0.909508)\) is displaced by \((0,1.0000000000287557\times10^{-6},0)\). The oxygen at \((0.593455,0.183947,0.114456)\) is displaced by \((1.0000000000287557\times10^{-6},0,1.000000000001\times10^{-6})\). The oxygen at \((0.069491,0.478999,0.885544)\) is displaced by \((0,0,-1.0000000000287557\times10^{-6})\). The oxygen at \((0.521001,0.406545,0.590492)\) is displaced by \((0,-9.999999999732445\times10^{-7},0)\). The oxygen at \((0.156545,0.066053,0.385544)\) is displaced by \((-1.000000000001\times10^{-6},0,-9.999999999732445\times10^{-7})\). Finally, the oxygen at \((0.680509,0.771001,0.614456)\) is displaced by \((0,0,1.0000000000287557\times10^{-6})\). These corrections are at the \(10^{-6}\) fractional-coordinate level and preserve the actual supplied input-cell geometry while remaining consistent with the stated standard-frame orbit description.
